texts.label: A
texts.title: Amira
texts.text: Amira runs a small graphic design studio from her home in Termiz. She started freelancing five years ago and now works with clients across Central Asia. She says the hardest part of running her own business was learning to manage her time, since nobody was telling her what to do each day. She now uses a strict weekly schedule and never works on Sundays, no matter how much work is waiting.

texts.label: B
texts.title: Sardor
texts.text: Sardor manages a logistics company that delivers goods between Surkhandarya and Tashkent. He took over the business from his father ten years ago and has since doubled the number of trucks. His biggest challenge has been finding reliable drivers, so he now offers extra training and a bonus system to keep good employees from leaving for competitors.

texts.label: C
texts.title: Nilufar
texts.text: Nilufar co-founded an online marketplace for local farmers to sell their produce directly to city customers, cutting out expensive middlemen. In the beginning, many farmers were suspicious of selling online and preferred traditional markets. Nilufar spent months visiting villages in person to explain how the platform worked before farmers started trusting it.

texts.label: D
texts.title: Bekzod
texts.text: Bekzod opened a language center offering English and business courses in his hometown. Demand grew so quickly that within a year he had to move to a bigger building and hire three more teachers. He believes the key to his success has been word-of-mouth recommendations from satisfied students rather than paid advertising.

parts.title: Part 3 — Matching Headings
parts.text:
Adapting to Remote Work

15) When offices around the world closed almost overnight, most companies had no formal policy for remote work at all. Managers who had always relied on walking over to a colleague's desk suddenly found themselves unable to gauge how their teams were really doing, and many admitted, in later interviews, that the first few weeks felt closer to guesswork than management.

16) Some companies responded by monitoring employees more closely, installing software that tracked keystrokes or took periodic screenshots. While this approach reassured a handful of nervous executives, employee surveys consistently showed that surveillance tools damaged trust far more than they improved output, often making staff feel like suspects rather than colleagues.

17) A smaller group of companies took the opposite approach, focusing entirely on results rather than hours logged. Managers set clear weekly goals and largely left employees to organize their own schedules. Early data suggested this approach worked well for experienced staff, though newer employees sometimes struggled without the informal guidance office life used to provide.

18) One unexpected challenge was the disappearance of casual, unplanned conversations — the kind that happen in a hallway or over coffee, rather than in a scheduled meeting. Several companies tried to recreate this with virtual "coffee chat" software, with mixed success; some employees found the forced scheduling made spontaneous conversation feel oddly artificial.

19) As remote work continued for months rather than weeks, a new concern emerged: many employees reported working longer hours than they had in the office, unable to draw a clear line between work and home life. Companies that ignored this often saw a rise in resignations several months later, once the initial novelty of working from home had worn off.

20) By the time many offices reopened, a significant number of employees requested to keep working remotely, at least part of the time. Businesses that treated the shift as temporary found themselves negotiating from a weaker position than those that had already begun redesigning their long-term policies around flexibility.

parts.title: Part 4 — Multiple Choice + True/False/No Info
parts.text:
The Unlikely Rise of a Local Bookshop

When Malika opened a small bookshop in Termiz eight years ago, most people in her family thought she was making a mistake. Online retailers had already begun undercutting small bookshops on price, and her own relatives suggested she open a clothing store instead, arguing that books were a dying business in the age of smartphones.

Malika disagreed, but not because she thought people would stop buying from online retailers entirely. Instead, she noticed that many of her friends complained about not knowing what to read next among the millions of titles available online. She decided her shop would sell something online retailers could not easily replicate: personal recommendations from someone who had actually read the books.

For the first two years, the shop barely broke even. Malika spent most evenings reading late into the night so she could speak knowledgeably about as many books as possible. Slowly, word spread that her recommendations were unusually accurate, and customers began returning specifically to ask, "What should I read next?" rather than searching for a specific title.

The shop's turning point came when Malika started a small monthly book club, initially just eight people meeting in the shop after closing hours. Members paid a small fee to join, which covered light refreshments, and Malika chose a different book each month based on the group's evolving tastes. Within eighteen months, the club had grown so large that she had to run two separate sessions to fit everyone in.

Today, book club memberships account for nearly a third of the shop's total income, and Malika has hired two part-time staff to help manage the growing membership. She still personally chooses every book club title herself, insisting that this personal touch is the one thing a large online retailer could never fully copy, no matter how sophisticated their recommendation algorithms become.

Scientists have spent a long time looking at why some people are early birds, while others are night owls. They looked at a medical database with genetic information for hundreds of thousands of (4)___. They compared the DNA of people who said they were early risers with the Neanderthal DNA. The (5)___ found more examples of Neanderthal DNA existed in the early risers. However, it is likely that the Neanderthal gene is not so strong in many people. 15) The world's first university was established in India in 700 BC, where more than 10,500 students from around the world studied more than 60 different subjects. The training was conducted in Sanskrit. Nowadays, Sanskrit is considered to be the mother of all the European languages. Its elements can be traced in most of them.

16) The most frequently visited place in India is Delhi, the capital city of the country. It seems to be divided into two parts. New Delhi is a modern city with hi-tech architecture, tourist attractions and modern facilities. Old Delhi is several centuries old, with narrow streets, ancient churches and noisy bazaars. Lots of people live in slums without the most essential facilities like toilets and running water.

17) People all over the world know of India's greatest river, the Ganges. The river looks extremely beautiful in the morning light. It is the subject of thousands of prayers. It has become a common ritual for pilgrims to gather by the holy river in the mornings. It is believed that bathing in the Ganges helps to cure all kinds of diseases and can improve your life in general.

18) Indian climate differs from one part of the country to another. The air is cool and fresh in the mountains, but in the plains it is usually very hot and dry, so even a short trip can be very hard for an inexperienced traveller. That is why tourists are always glad to have a rest at one of the numerous stations in the hills. There they can enjoy a nice cup of real Indian tea, the most refreshing drink in such a climate.

19) India is not all history. It is also famous for its Bollywood industry, which produces different films. Indian films have always had their own style; they are rich in music and dancing. Though the industry is still developing, many Indian film stars have received Oscar prizes and are known throughout the world. The home of Bollywood is Mumbai, also known as a busy port and the country's commercial centre.

20) There is an unusual treasure hidden in the Indian mountains. These are striking ancient temples cut in the rocks. For example, the Buddhist cave temples at Ajanta were built at least 2,000 years ago. Inside the caves on the walls, tourists can see animal images and pictures of people's lives. Some researchers believe that the interpretation of the images can help us to learn a lot about people's lives in ancient times.

parts.title: Part 4 — Multiple Choice + True/False/No Info
parts.text:
PIRATES

There have always been people who robbed ships in the open sea. We know them as pirates or corsairs. Many of them were sailors who lost their jobs, others were just young men and women looking for adventure. Thousands of pirates were active from 1650–1720. These years are sometimes known as the 'Golden Age' of piracy. Probably the most famous pirates of this period are Blackbeard, Henry Morgan, William 'Captain' Kidd, and the Barbarossa brothers.

The "Jolly Roger" is the well-known pirate flag. There are a number of theories about its origin. It is thought that the first pirates used a red flag, which was common in sea attacks. A red flag told other ships that there would be no pity and no prisoners would be taken. This red flag was called Joli Rouge (pretty red) in French. Most probably, English people pronounced it in their own way "Jolly Roger". Another theory says that "old Roger" was another name for the devil.

Another popular image from the pirate world is a parrot, sitting on the captain's shoulder. Well, there's no historical proof of that. No doubt, pirates often travelled to faraway exotic lands and brought unusual animals as souvenirs with them. Parrots were particularly popular because they were colourful, could be taught to speak, and were easier to care for than, say, monkeys. However, you can't imagine a pirate fighting with a bird on the shoulder. This image possibly began with the book "Treasure Island". In the book, the ever famous Long John Silver carried a parrot as a pet.

Before joining a ship each pirate signed an agreement called "Articles". This explained the rights and laws on board the ship, how much a person was paid, what to do in case of emergency, etc. For example, playing cards for money was not allowed. For breaking the rules a pirate would be shot or left on a desert island with a bottle of water and a gun.

A pirate ship was organized democratically. After a successful attack they divided the treasures equally, only the captain and the cook got more. They sometimes decided together which ship to attack or where to sail next. Most pirates were paid four times more than they had when they were sailors. But on land they were criminals and lots of money was offered to those who caught them.

However, for some time the English government supported pirates. There were lots of pirates in the sixteenth century when England was at war with Spain and the Dutch Republic. Queen Elizabeth I ordered them to rob Spanish ships and bring gold, silver and jewels to the country. Sir Francis Drake was one of the most famous pirates. He brought lots of treasures to England and also was the first Englishman to sail all the way around the world. Because of this, he was made a knight by Queen Elizabeth I.

parts.title: Part 5 — Note Completion
parts.textTemplate:
IS GRAFFITI ART OR CRIME?

The term graffiti derives from the Italian graffito meaning 'scratching' and can be defined as uninvited marking or writing scratched or applied to objects, built structures and natural features. It is not a new phenomenon: examples can be found on ancient structures around the world, in some cases predating the Greeks and Romans. In such circumstances it has acquired invaluable historical and archaeological significance, providing a social history of life and events at that time.

It is usually considered a priority to remove graffiti as quickly as possible after it appears, partly to prevent 'copy-cat' emulation, and because it may be of a racist or otherwise offensive nature. The police should be informed as there may be other related attacks occurring locally; stylised signatures or nicknames, known as 'tags', may already be familiar to local police.

Operatives ought to comply with relevant health and safety rules during removal, following product guidelines and wearing the appropriate protective equipment.

One of the most significant problems associated with graffiti removal is the need to remove it from surfaces that are repeatedly attacked, which can ultimately damage the surface material. Anti-graffiti coatings are usually applied by brush or spray, leaving a thin veneer that isolates the graffiti from the surface. Removal of graffiti from a surface that has been treated in this way is much easier, usually using low-pressure water, which reduces the possibility of damage.
